Preventive Dentistry

Gum Disease: Early Signs, Treatment, and Prevention

Learn how gum disease develops, which signs deserve attention, and how daily care and professional treatment help protect supporting tissues.

August 25, 20263 min readPublished by The House of Dental

Gum disease often begins quietly

Plaque is a sticky film of bacteria that forms on teeth each day. When it is not removed, the gums can become inflamed. Early gum disease, called gingivitis, may cause redness, swelling, tenderness, or bleeding during brushing and cleaning between teeth.

Bleeding gums are common, but they are not something to ignore. Gingivitis can often improve when plaque is removed consistently and a professional cleaning addresses hardened deposits. If inflammation spreads deeper, it can damage the ligament and bone that support the teeth. That stage is called periodontitis.

Symptoms do not always show the severity

Periodontitis may cause persistent bad breath, receding gums, spaces that appear between teeth, tenderness while chewing, or teeth that feel mobile. Some people have little pain even when bone loss is present. A periodontal examination measures the spaces around the teeth and looks for bleeding, recession, mobility, and changes on dental images.

Several factors can increase risk or complicate healing. Tobacco use is a major one. Diabetes, some medications, genetics, age, and conditions that affect immune response can also matter. Risk does not confirm disease, but it can influence how often someone needs evaluation and maintenance.

Treatment depends on how far disease has progressed

Gingivitis may improve with professional cleaning and more effective daily plaque removal. Periodontitis usually requires cleaning below the gumline. Scaling removes plaque and hardened calculus, while root planing smooths contaminated root surfaces so the tissues can heal more predictably.

Deeper or more complex disease may need periodontal surgery or care from a specialist. Treatment does not end when the initial inflammation settles. Periodontal maintenance visits are scheduled according to risk because bacteria can repopulate below the gumline and the disease can return.

Prevention is mostly consistent, ordinary work

Brush twice a day with fluoride toothpaste and clean between the teeth regularly using floss, an interdental brush, or another method recommended for the spaces in your mouth. Technique matters more than force. Aggressive scrubbing can injure the gums without cleaning the difficult areas any better.

Routine dental visits allow plaque, calculus, and tissue changes to be found before they are obvious at home. Anyone who notices repeated bleeding, gum recession, persistent odor, swelling, or tooth movement should arrange an evaluation instead of waiting for pain.

Why maintenance intervals differ

A six-month visit is familiar, but it is not the right interval for every mouth. Someone with a history of periodontitis may need maintenance more often because deeper areas can become inflamed again before a routine schedule catches them. The interval can change as health, home care, and disease stability change.

Maintenance is also a chance to adjust the daily routine. Recession, bridges, implants, crowded teeth, and limited hand dexterity may call for different brushes or interdental tools. The best method is one that reaches the actual problem areas and can be repeated consistently.

Gum disease management is measured over time. Less bleeding and shallower pockets can show improvement, while new recession, pus, mobility, or continuing bone loss may signal that the plan needs to change. Keeping those measurements from visit to visit is more informative than judging the gums by appearance alone or waiting for pain to appear.

Sources and further reading

  1. National Institute of Dental and Craniofacial Research: Gum Disease
  2. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention: About Periodontal Disease
